title: Song of Solomon 5:1–8
context: In the WEB headings, the Lover answers the invitation of 4:16 and the Friends call the couple to eat and drink (5:1). The Beloved then tells of a night when she delayed opening to her beloved, found him gone, searched the city, was mistreated by the watchmen, and charged the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is faint with love (5:2–8). Many read 5:2–8 as dreamlike. The scene is read both literally and allegorically within both traditions.

verses.text: I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends! Drink, yes, drink abundantly, beloved.
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB headings give the Lover’s words, “I have come into my garden,” then the Friends’ call, “Eat, friends! Drink, yes, drink abundantly, beloved.” Arminian readers see love fulfilled and celebrated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lover answering the invitation of 4:16. Readers in this tradition note that the identity of the final speaker is debated, and they hold the WEB heading as one reasonable reading.

verses.text: I was asleep, but my heart was awake. It is the voice of my beloved who knocks: “Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled; for my head is filled with dew, and my hair with the dampness of the night.”
verses.arminianNotes: Under the heading Beloved: “I was asleep, but my heart was awake.” She hears “the voice of my beloved who knocks.” Arminian readers see a scene of longing and hesitation, told with dreamlike language.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a vivid, perhaps dreamlike, scene. Allegorical readers often compare the knocking with Revelation 3:20, while literal readers see a lover’s night visit; readers in this tradition do not force one view.

verses.text: I have taken off my robe. Indeed, must I put it on? I have washed my feet. Indeed, must I soil them?
verses.arminianNotes: “I have taken off my robe. Indeed, must I put it on?” Arminian readers see reluctance and delay in responding to the beloved’s call, a theme many apply to spiritual sluggishness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see hesitation that will lead to loss. Allegorical readers apply it to coldness toward Christ, while literal readers see the ups and downs of human love; both approaches are held in this tradition.

verses.text: My beloved thrust his hand in through the latch opening. My heart pounded for him.
verses.arminianNotes: “My beloved thrust his hand in through the latch opening. My heart pounded for him.” Arminian readers see the beloved’s persistence awakening her response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see her heart stirred by his approach. The scene is told with restraint, and readers in this tradition keep their comments modest in line with the poem’s own reticence.

verses.text: I rose up to open for my beloved. My hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the lock.
verses.arminianNotes: “I rose up to open for my beloved.” Her hands drip with myrrh on the handles of the lock. Arminian readers see her finally responding, though the delay will cost her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a belated response. The detail of myrrh adds fragrance to the scene, and readers in this tradition do not press any further symbolism onto it.

verses.text: I opened to my beloved; but my beloved left, and had gone away. My heart went out when he spoke. I looked for him, but I didn’t find him. I called him, but he didn’t answer.
verses.arminianNotes: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved left, and had gone away.” Arminian readers see the pain of a missed moment, which many apply to the seriousness of answering love promptly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see absence and searching. Allegorical readers have applied this to seasons when God’s presence seems withdrawn, while literal readers see lovers’ separation; readers in this tradition hold both.

verses.text: The watchmen who go about the city found me. They beat me. They bruised me. The keepers of the walls took my cloak away from me.
verses.arminianNotes: “The watchmen who go about the city found me. They beat me.” Arminian readers note the painful turn of the scene and read it soberly as part of the beloved’s distress in searching.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat this harsh moment with restraint. The text does not explain why the watchmen act as they do, and readers in this tradition avoid speculation about their motives.

verses.text: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, If you find my beloved, that you tell him that I am faint with love.
verses.arminianNotes: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, If you find my beloved, that you tell him that I am faint with love.” Arminian readers see longing that seeks help from others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the beloved’s earnest appeal. The charge to the daughters of Jerusalem recurs in the Song, and here it expresses love sick with longing rather than the restraint urged in 2:7.
